How every device on the Internet is identified: the 32 bits of an IP address, which part names the network and which the host, what the mask is for, and how the address space was allocated.
Why an IP address is needed in addition to the MAC
How to read a 32-bit address and what the mask indicates
What the network address and the broadcast address mean (and why 254 hosts remain)
How IANA divided the space into classes A, B, C, D and E
What private addresses (RFC 1918) are, and classless addressing with prefixes

IP, as a layer 3 protocol, solves two things: addressing and routing.

Addressing makes it possible to reach a destination that is on another network. Two pieces of data are needed: the destination address and the source address, so the reply can come back.

It is like a letter: on one side you write who the recipient is and where they are; on the other, who I am and where I am.
Each datagram carries a unique identifier for the sender and another for the recipient.
The destination address is what gets the datagram there; the source address is what lets the other side reply. Both travel in the header of every datagram.

The identifier chosen has 32 bits: about 4.3 billion combinations. IP was born from a request by the U.S. Department of Defense; nobody imagined it would become the Internet protocol, and 32 bits seemed to cover any future need.

It is written as 4 bytes separated by dots, each with its decimal value (0 to 255): for example 24.32.218.197.

That way everyone has a different identifier, with no ambiguity.
An IPv4 address is 32 bits; dotted notation is just a convenient way to write them.
An IP address, bit by bit
Each group of 8 bits is written as its decimal value. The first: 00011000 = 16 + 8 = 24. The last: 11000101 = 128 + 64 + 4 + 1 = 197.

Inside the LAN, stations talk to each other by MAC address. But the MAC is no use for communicating with devices outside the network: each station also needs an IP address to get out and receive replies.

The 32 bits have two parts:

  • Network: the same for all devices on the same network.
  • Host (any addressable device): different for each one.

Like on a street: all the houses share the street and each has its own number.
Same network identifier for all; a different host identifier for each.

Street = network: 200.10.1
Number = host: 100, 101, 102
Two houses cannot have the same number.

The mask says which part of the address is network and which part is host. It has 32 bits, just like the IP: each bit of the address has a corresponding bit in the mask.

Rule: the ones all go together at the start (network) and the zeros all together at the end (host). There can be no interleaved ones.

If the first three octets are network, each is 11111111 = 255 and the last is 00000000 = 0: 255.255.255.0. In 200.10.1.100, 200.10.1 is the network and 100 the host.
Mask bit set to 1 → that IP bit is network. Set to 0 → it is host.
IP and mask, aligned bit by bit
When you configure an IP on a device, you are always asked for the subnet mask as well: without it there is no way to know where the network ends and the host begins.
All zeros is the network, all ones is broadcast

All hosts on the network start with 200.10.1; what changes is the last 8 bits: 256 combinations (0 to 255).

Two of them cannot be assigned to a device:

  • Host all 0s (200.10.1.0): identifies the network as a whole.
  • Host all 1s (200.10.1.255): it is the broadcast.

That leaves 254 valid addresses to use inside the network.
Usable hosts = 2 to the number of host bits, minus 2.
.0 is reserved: it names the whole network.
.255 is reserved: it is the network's broadcast.
IANA splits the space in half

With the Internet came IANA, which manages the IPv4 address space: a company said how many devices it had and received a network address.

To allocate, IANA splits the space into blocks, always in half. Addresses starting with bit 0 are class A. The half starting with 1 is split again: 10 is class B; then 110 is C, 1110 is D and 1111 is E.
Looking at the first octet tells you the class: A 0–127, B 128–191, C 192–223.
IPv4 space by first-octet value (0 to 255)
2 · The half with 1 is split again
Classes A, B, C, D and E

Each class fixes how many bits are network and how many are host:

  • A (large networks): 8 network and 24 host. With the first bit fixed, 2⁷ networks remain.
  • B (medium): 16 and 16. Two fixed bits → 2¹⁴ networks.
  • C (small): 24 and 8. Three fixed bits → 2²¹ networks of 2⁸ addresses.
  • D: multicast. E: reserved for future use.
The more bits used for the network, the more networks there are and the smaller each one is.
The 32 bits of each class (bit 0 to bit 31)
Class A · first octet 0 – 127 · 2^7 = 128 networks · 2^24 ≈ 16 million hosts per network
Class B · 128 – 191 · 2^14 ≈ 16 thousand networks · 2^16 ≈ 64 thousand hosts per network
Class C · 192 – 223 · 2^21 ≈ 2 million networks · 2^8 = 256 hosts per network
Class E · 240 – 255 · reserved for future use

Requests keep growing and fewer and fewer addresses remain available. The answer is RFC 1918: blocks of class A, B and C are reserved for private use.

Any company can use them freely to build its internal TCP/IP networks.

In exchange, these addresses cannot enter the Internet: there, uniqueness must be respected, and many companies will repeat the same ones.
A private address can repeat in thousands of networks; that is why it cannot circulate on the Internet.

Later it was decided to eliminate classes: this is classless addressing. IANA is no longer tied to network identifiers of 8, 16 or 24 bits: it can hand out, for example, a block with 22 bits of network.

Flexibility is gained: a block can be a fragment of one class, or combine fragments of more than one.

The fixed bits are called the prefix. The mask gives the prefix length, written /22.
Prefix = the fixed bits of a block. Its length is the number of ones in the mask.
With classes, the network / host boundary could only fall at bit 8, 16 or 24. With classless it can fall at any bit: here, in the middle of the third octet.

• IP address: 32 bits, 4 octets in decimal.
  • Two parts: network (shared) and host (unique). The mask marks the boundary with contiguous ones.
  • Host all 0s = the network; all 1s = broadcast. Usable: 2ⁿ − 2.
  • Classes A, B, C (0, 10, 110), D multicast, E reserved.
  • RFC 1918: private addresses that don't enter the Internet.
  • Classless: prefixes of any length.

If the prefix can have any length, we can also lengthen it ourselves: in the next lesson we split a block into subnets.
First octet: 200 falls in the class C block
A host has IP 200.10.1.100 with mask 255.255.255.0. Which is the network part and which is the host part?
The mask has 24 consecutive ones: the first three octets are network and the last one is the host.
On that same network, how many addresses can be assigned to devices?
With 8 host bits there are 256 combinations, but all 0s identifies the network and all 1s is the broadcast: 254 remain.
An address starts with bits 10 (first octet between 128 and 191). Which class does it belong to?
Class A starts with 0, B with 10, C with 110 and D with 1110. B uses 16 network bits and 16 host bits.
What characterizes RFC 1918 addresses, such as 192.168.0.10?
They are the only ones that can be used on the Internet
Anyone can use them on their internal network, but they cannot enter the Internet
Only IANA can assign them, to large companies
They are private-use blocks: they repeat across many internal networks, so they do not meet the uniqueness that the Internet requires.
32 bits in 4 decimal octets (0–255). About 4.3 billion combinations.
The network part is common to all devices on the network; the host part is unique to each.
32 bits: contiguous ones at the start (network) and zeros at the end (host). E.g.: 255.255.255.0 = /24.
Host all 0s = the network; host all 1s = broadcast. Usable hosts = 2ⁿ − 2 (with 8 bits: 254).
A: 2⁷ networks of 2²⁴ hosts · B: 2¹⁴ of 2¹⁶ · C: 2²¹ of 2⁸.
Private: 10/8, 172.16/12 and 192.168/16. They cannot enter the Internet.
No class boundaries: the prefix (fixed bits) can have any length, e.g. /22.
